title: Jewish humor
hook: laughter as a way of surviving

segments.voice: Yesterday, interfaith families, and the line families are complex. Did you ask one more question before deciding? These last few days have been about who belongs: Jews by choice, every face, cultural Jews, families with two traditions. Today, the week ends with a laugh. Day one thousand fifty.

A man is rescued after years alone on a desert island. His rescuers look around and find he's built himself two synagogues. Why two, they ask. He points. This one I go to. That one, I wouldn't set foot in. People tell that joke at Jewish tables, and they tell it about themselves. It's warm, it's a little sharp, and it's true enough to sting. It also hides something serious. A people that has lived through exile, expulsions and grief kept something in its pocket the whole time: the ability to laugh, including at itself. Today's word is that laughter.
screen: `TWO SYNAGOGUES ON ONE ISLAND.` → `A JOKE TOLD ABOUT OURSELVES.` → `LAUGHTER KEPT IN THE POCKET.`

segments.voice: Laughter shows up early in the Torah, and in an unexpected place. Sarah, old and long past hoping, overhears a visitor tell Abraham she'll have a son. She laughs to herself. When the child is born, she says that God has made laughter for her, and everyone who hears will laugh with her. The boy is named Yitzchak, Isaac, and readers have long heard laughter in that name. So one of the founding families of the people carries a joke in its own name: a promise so unlikely that the only honest answer was to laugh. The Psalms remember laughter at the other end of a hard road. A psalm about coming home from captivity says: "Then was our mouth filled with laughter." Not after everything was fixed. At the moment of return, still dusty. And the Talmud tells a small, lovely story. A rabbi named Beroka is standing in a crowded market with the prophet Elijah, and asks him: is anyone here destined for the world to come? Elijah points to two ordinary men. The rabbi goes and asks what they do. They say: we're jesters. When we see someone sad, we cheer them up. When we see two people quarreling, we work to make peace between them. In that whole crowded market, these two are among the very few Elijah points to. That's the root of today's line. In this tradition, humor at its best isn't a way of hiding from pain. It's a way of carrying it, and of carrying each other. A joke can let a frightened room breathe. It can puncture the pompous and spare the weak. It can say, we're still here. Today's line is one word: laugh.
screen: `SARAH LAUGHS.` · `THEN WAS OUR MOUTH FILLED WITH LAUGHTER.` · `TWO JESTERS IN THE MARKET.` · `HUMOR THAT CARRIES PAIN.` · then, large: `LAUGH.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: tell one gentle joke. First, settle and breathe. Let your shoulders drop. Now go looking, in memory, for something that made you laugh: a family story, a line a friend said, something a child got gloriously wrong. Choose one that makes nobody smaller. The best ones laugh at life, or at ourselves. Hold it, and notice what it does to your face just to remember it. Then think of one person who could use it today, someone tired, or sad, or in the middle of a quarrel. Like the jesters in the market, you're carrying it to them. The bell holds the time.
Jewish humor. Laughter carried through hard times, aimed at life and at oneself, and honored in the Talmud's story of the two jesters. Today's word.
Your line: laugh. Today, tell that gentle joke to the person who needs it, and laugh with them, not at anyone. Day one thousand fifty.

howItsDone: Jewish humor lives in family stories, folk tales, Yiddish and Ladino sayings, holiday spoofs such as Purim plays, and in writers and comedians, and it is often told by Jews about themselves.

notes: Week-end look-back (days 1044–1050) in the review. Day 1045's carry ('fifteen million') is not repeated, per the claims rule.
The desert-island joke is a widely told folk joke Jews tell about themselves; please confirm it is appropriate (it is about communal argument, not belief).
Isaac's name: phrased as 'readers have long heard laughter in that name' rather than a stated etymology. The Torah itself links the name and laughter (Genesis 17:17–19; 21:6). Please confirm.
Genesis 21:6 is paraphrased (not quoted). Psalm 126:2 JPS 1917 wording should be checked word for word.
Taanit 22a (Rabbi Beroka, Elijah and the jesters) paraphrased; Elijah also points to a jailer earlier in the passage, omitted here. Please confirm.
'Laughter kept in the pocket' and 'humor at its best... carrying it' are framed as this tradition's stories, not as claims about all Jews.
